open-question.question: The mission page is to show one button per recipe with selectable variants, each variant a literal block of command lines. The shipped file `snippets/GURITA_USAGE.md` holds every block as a recipe of its own under a `###` heading, a chain's Antigravity copy being a separate recipe whose heading ends in `(Antigravity)`, and the recipe reader groups no two recipes. How does the shipped file express that several blocks are variants of one recipe, each under a name of its own?
open-question.alternative: Each recipe is one `###` heading whose name is the recipe's name, with its optional `Stage:` line beneath it once for the whole recipe, and each variant is a `####` sub-heading naming the variant followed by that variant's fenced block. Because a recipe's variants on both harnesses then stand under one heading, the `## Claude Code` and `## Antigravity` recipe sections become one recipe section, the Antigravity notes kept there as prose, and the `(Antigravity)` heading suffixes go. A recipe with one block and no `####` is a recipe of one variant, so the button recipes and the single-task lines keep their `###` headings, and the names the rule file and the preview's override list use, as they are. The grouping and every variant's name are visible structure in the rendered Markdown and its outline, so the file still reads as a document a person copies chains from, each variant labelled where it stands, and the reader finds a variant by a heading level it already parses headings at. The reader gains a second heading level and the shipped file is restructured whole (sections merged, every chain's copies moved under one heading), so the README, the two tests that read the shipped file, and the reader's group logic all change; whether the own recipe file takes the same form is the variant store and own-recipe siblings' to settle.

Each recipe is one `###` heading carrying the recipe's name and its optional `Stage:` line once, and each variant is a `Variant: name` line standing at column 0 outside any fence, followed by that variant's fenced block, the same kind of marker the reader already reads for `Stage:`. The two host recipe sections become one recipe section and the `(Antigravity)` heading suffixes go. A recipe with a single block and no `Variant:` line is a recipe of one variant, so the button recipes and single-task lines keep their headings and names unchanged. It extends the one marker convention the file and reader already have (a column-0 keyword line between heading and fence) rather than adding a heading level, so the parse stays line-based and a variant name is free text with no Markdown structure of its own. In rendered Markdown a variant's name is a plain paragraph line easily read as prose rather than as a label, and the file is still restructured whole (sections merged, copies regrouped), with the README, the reader, and the tests reading the shipped file changed alongside.

Each recipe is one `###` heading with its optional `Stage:` line once, holding several fenced blocks, each block's variant name written in its opening fence's info string (for example a fence opened as three backticks followed by `variant=Antigravity`). The reader takes every fence under the heading rather than only the first, the two host recipe sections become one, and the `(Antigravity)` suffixes go; a heading with one unnamed fence is a recipe of one variant, keeping the button recipes' and single-task lines' names as they are. Each variant's name travels inside its own block, so a block can never be separated from its name, and the file's visible prose and heading structure barely change beyond the regrouping. Rendered Markdown hides the info string, so a person reading or copying from the shipped file sees several unlabelled blocks under one heading, and the info string is conventionally a language tag that some renderers treat as one, which makes the format fragile and its rule hard to discover.

Every block stays a `###` recipe of its own under its own heading in its host section, as today, its heading now the variant's name, and a new column-0 line between heading and fence, such as `Recipe: First run`, names the recipe it is a variant of, beside the `Stage:` line; the reader groups every block that declares the same recipe name into one recipe, and a block declaring none is a recipe of one variant. The `## Claude Code` and `## Antigravity` sections and every existing heading stay as written. The smallest change to the file: no block moves, every heading stays a unique name, so the rule file, the override list, and replacement by name keep their one identifier per block, and the reader only adds one more marker beside the one it reads. A recipe's variants stand scattered across the two host sections with nothing in the rendered file showing they belong together, each repeats its own `Stage:` line that can disagree with its siblings', and a variant's name is its full heading (`First run (Antigravity)`) unless a second name line is added; how replacement by name then works is the own-recipe sibling's to settle.

The file gets no new syntax and stays as it stands: the reader groups recipes by their heading with a trailing parenthetical stripped, so `First run` and `First run (Antigravity)` form the recipe `First run`, the parenthetical naming the variant and a heading without one taking its host section's name (`Claude Code`) as its variant name. Nothing in the shipped file changes, so the document a person reads, the README's description of it, and the tests reading it stay valid, and the grouping is inferred from the naming the file already follows. The rule is implicit and catches headings never meant as variants: `Execute tasks (critical tasks)` would group under `Execute tasks`, and `Single task with Opus High (Claude Code)` with its Antigravity copy would merge into one recipe, breaking the heading names the rule file and the preview's override list look single-task lines up by unless they are exempted by a further rule; whether the execution recipes are to merge at all is the execution-recipes sibling's to settle.

The `(Antigravity)` suffix is dropped from the chain headings, so each chain's copies carry the same `###` heading, one under `## Claude Code` and one under `## Antigravity`; the reader groups same-named recipes across the two host sections into one recipe and names each variant by the host section it stands in. The single-task lines keep their distinct headings, since the rule file names them, and every other recipe stays as written. The file keeps its host sections and Markdown shape, the change to it is a handful of heading edits, and a variant's name comes from a heading already visible in the rendered file. A recipe can hold at most one variant per host section, so two variants on one harness, or a chain mixing `agy` and `claude` lines, have no place without a second marker, and the same name standing twice makes a name no longer identify one block for replacement by name; how the execution recipes and the mixed-agent chain are placed is their siblings' to settle.

The shipped file stays exactly as written, and which shipped blocks are variants of one recipe, and each variant's name, are held outside it, in a fixed table in the extension's code or in a bundled sidecar file beside `bundled/GURITA_USAGE.md`, that maps each shipped heading to its recipe and variant name; a heading the table does not name is a recipe of one variant. The file stays a plain document of copyable chains with no extension-specific markup, and every heading keeps its one name, so the rule file, replacement by name, and the tests reading the shipped file are untouched. The grouping lives apart from the blocks it groups, so renaming or adding a shipped chain needs a matching table edit that nothing ties to the file, and a person's own recipe file has no way to express variants of its own unless it gains a format after all.

The shipped file expresses no grouping and stays as written: every shipped block remains a recipe of one variant under its own heading, `First run` and `First run (Antigravity)` remaining two recipes and two buttons, and a recipe gains further variants only through the settings view's duplicates in the per-user store. Nothing in the shipped file, its reader, or its tests changes, and the variant mechanism is built once, in the per-user store the settings view writes, rather than twice. The page keeps a separate button per harness copy of each chain, so the goal's one button per recipe holds only for recipes a person has duplicated, and a person switching a chain between Claude Code and Antigravity still chooses between two buttons rather than two variants.

open-question.question: The settings view holds a model list and an effort list for each harness, and no file of the extension or the plugin lists them today: `claude` has no command that prints its models, while `agy models` prints one line per pair of model and effort. Where do the lists come from (values shipped with the extension, the values the recipe lines carry, a query of the harness, or the person's own entries), and can the person add and remove entries?
open-question.alternative: Source: each harness's lists are read from the `--model` and `--effort` values the shipped recipes', own recipes', and stored variants' lines carry, as in the fixed form. Editing: the person can add entries no line yet uses and remove derived entries from the offer; the additions and removals are stored per user as an overlay on the derived lists. Keeps the extension free of shipped model names and keeps the lists tied to what is actually run, while letting the person reach a new model or effort without hand-editing a recipe file first. The first open offers only what the shipped lines use, so the person must type every other value themselves, a removed derived entry reappears in any new line that carries it unless the removal is kept as a standing hide rule, and the overlay needs a per-user store (the Harness state store question's).

Source: the extension ships one model list and one effort list per harness as a constant in its own code or a bundled file (for `claude` the aliases `fable`, `opus`, `sonnet` and the efforts low, medium, high, xhigh, max that `claude --help` gives; for `agy` the base model ids and efforts `agy models` printed on 2026-11-22). Editing: none; the person cannot add or remove entries, and the lists change only with a new extension release. The simplest and most predictable form: no process is started to build a list, nothing extra is stored per user, the lists are identical on every machine and pinned by the extension's unit tests, and they work when a harness is absent or its query fails. The lists go stale as soon as a harness adds or retires a model (`agy models` already lists models no recipe uses), a full `claude` model name or a newly released model cannot be chosen without a release, and the extension now holds model names and effort levels, which the design draft recorded it would not (a revision the Design draft revision question owns).

Source: the extension ships one model list and one effort list per harness, as in the fixed form. Editing: the person can add entries and remove entries in the settings view; the additions and the removals are stored per user as an overlay on the shipped lists, so the list shown is the shipped list minus the person's removals plus the person's additions, and a shipped entry added by a later release appears unless the person removed it. Gives a working list on first open with no setup and no harness query, lets the person reach a model or full name the shipped list lacks or hide one never used, and still lets later releases' corrections reach every person. Two layers to merge and explain (a removed shipped entry must be remembered as a removal, and an added entry that a release later ships becomes a duplicate to fold), a per-user store for the overlay (where it lives is the Harness state store question's), and the shipped part still goes stale between releases and places model names in the extension.

Source: the extension ships one model list and one effort list per harness, used only to fill a person's lists the first time the settings view needs them. Editing: from then on the lists are the person's own stored copy, every entry added or removed freely, and no later shipped list changes it. One plain list per harness that the person fully owns, with no overlay rules: what the settings view shows is exactly what is stored, and the first open still offers sensible values. A later release's corrected or extended list never reaches a person whose copy already exists unless a reset is added, so lists drift apart across machines and versions, and the copy needs a per-user store (the Harness state store question's).

Source: no list is shipped or stored; each harness's model list and effort list is read afresh, on every re-read of the pane, from the `--model` and `--effort` values the lines of the shipped recipes, the person's own recipes, and the stored variants carry, grouped by each line's harness. Editing: none; an entry appears or disappears only as lines using it are added, edited, or deleted. Nothing new to maintain or store and nothing to go stale on its own: the lists are always exactly the values the person's runs already use, and the extension still writes down no model name or effort level of its own. Only values some line already carries can be chosen, so a model or effort no line uses (`gemini-4-neon`, `low`, `max`) is unreachable from the settings view and must first be written into an own recipe by hand, and deleting the last variant using a value removes it from the list; the values found depend on reading each line, which the Unreadable lines question governs.

Source: each harness's lists are the union of a list the extension ships per harness and the `--model` and `--effort` values the shipped recipes', own recipes', and stored variants' lines carry, so a value an own recipe uses (a full `claude` model name, say) is offered without being shipped. Editing: the person can add and remove entries, the additions and removals stored per user as an overlay on the merged lists. The widest offer with the least typing: the shipped part covers values no line uses yet, the derived part picks up whatever a person's own lines already run, and the overlay covers the rest. Three sources to merge, with the most rules to state, test, and explain (which removal hides which source, how a derived value that is also shipped is shown), the shipped part still goes stale between releases, and the overlay needs a per-user store (the Harness state store question's).

Source: Antigravity's lists are read from `agy models`, its `id<TAB>name` lines split into each base model id and the efforts it is printed at; Claude Code's lists, which no `claude` command prints, are shipped with the extension (the aliases and the efforts `claude --help` gives). Editing: none. Antigravity's list is exact and current on the person's own machine, including which efforts each model takes, so a line is never offered a model the installed harness lacks, with no list for it to maintain anywhere. Two mechanisms per harness; the query starts an `agy` process (when and through what shell are the Harness check timing and Harness check shell questions'), depends on an unversioned print format, and yields no list when `agy` is absent or fails; Claude Code's half still goes stale and cannot reach a full model name; whether the per-model efforts the query gives are kept per model is the Effort list granularity question's.

alternative.id: Antigravity query, shipped Claude, person overlay

open-question.alternative: Source: Antigravity's lists are read from `agy models` and Claude Code's are shipped with the extension, as in the fixed form. Editing: the person can add and remove entries on either harness, the additions and removals stored per user as an overlay on the queried or shipped lists. Each harness gets the most accurate source it has, and the overlay closes the gaps both leave: a full or newly released `claude` model name, or an `agy` entry to hide or to keep when the query is unavailable. The most moving parts of any option: a harness process per query with its own timing and shell (the Harness check timing and Harness check shell questions'), an unversioned print format, a shipped half that goes stale, an overlay over two kinds of source, and a per-user store (the Harness state store question's).

alternative.id: Antigravity query, Claude recipe values, person overlay

open-question.alternative: Source: Antigravity's lists are read from `agy models`; Claude Code's are read from the `--model` and `--effort` values that the `claude` lines of the shipped recipes, own recipes, and stored variants carry, so the extension ships no model name or effort level for either harness. Editing: the person can add and remove entries on either harness, the additions and removals stored per user as an overlay. Keeps the design draft's rule that the extension holds no model name or effort level, while Antigravity's list stays exact from the harness itself and Claude Code's grows from what is run plus what the person enters. Claude Code offers only the values its lines already use (no `low` or `max`, no full model name) until the person types more, the `agy` query brings its process, timing, shell, and print-format dependencies (the Harness check timing and Harness check shell questions'), and the overlay needs a per-user store (the Harness state store question's).

Source: nothing is shipped, read from lines, or queried; each harness's model list and effort list starts empty and holds only what the person enters in the settings view. Editing: the person adds and removes every entry. The extension holds no model name or effort level and runs no query, so nothing it carries can go stale, and each list is exactly the person's deliberate choice with one store and no merge rules. The settings view offers nothing until the person has typed every model and effort by hand, so a first-time person cannot change a line's model or effort without first learning the harness's names from its own help, and a mistyped entry is only found when a line using it stops at run time; it needs a per-user store (the Harness state store question's).

open-question.question: The shipped recipe file holds `Execute tasks of normal difficulty` and `Execute tasks (critical tasks)` as two recipes, each with an Antigravity copy, whose one `complete-all-tasks` line differs only in effort, the Antigravity critical copy running its line on `claude`. Once a recipe carries variants, do the two stay separate recipes, each with its own variants, or become variants of one execution recipe?
open-question.alternative: The two become one execution recipe under a single name, replacing both present names, and its variants are every distinct line the four shipped copies hold: Claude Code at `high` (`opus`), Antigravity at `high` (`claude-opus-5-5`), and Claude Code at `xhigh` (`opus`). The Antigravity critical copy repeats the last line, so it is dropped. `Execute tasks one at a time` stays a recipe of its own. It fits the model the goal describes. The shipped lines differ only in harness, model, and effort, which are exactly what a variant varies, what the button label shows, and what the settings view edits per line. Difficulty becomes one more variant a person can duplicate and retune, and the execute-tasks step shows one button for `complete-all-tasks`. Difficulty moves into a dropdown whose choice is remembered, so one click runs whatever was selected last time. Running at critical effort, or dropping back to normal effort, becomes a choice that is easy to leave stale. Both present names disappear, so an own recipe carrying either name no longer stands in for a shipped one, depending on how the own-recipe replacement question is settled. The merged recipe needs a new name, and its variants need names of their own.

The two stay separate recipes under their present names, and the host copies become their variants. `Execute tasks of normal difficulty` holds two variants: the Claude Code line (`opus` at `high`) and the Antigravity line (`claude-opus-5-5` at `high`). `Execute tasks (critical tasks)` holds a single variant, the Claude Code line at `xhigh`. Its Antigravity copy runs that same `claude` line, so it is dropped rather than kept as a duplicate variant. `Execute tasks one at a time` stays a recipe of its own. Difficulty stays a choice of which button to press, decided per click and never carried over by a remembered dropdown selection, so a critical run cannot silently run at `high`, or a routine run at `xhigh`, because of an earlier choice. Both names stay the same, so a hand-written own recipe carrying either name still matches it, and the split matches the critical-versus-normal split the rule file already draws for single-task lines. One skill run at two efforts takes up two buttons on the execute-tasks step, three with the looped run. The critical recipe's dropdown offers only one variant, so the variant mechanism does nothing for it. Any further effort a person adds in the settings view has to go under one of the two difficulty names or into a recipe of its own, which reproduces the per-effort split that variants were meant to fold away.

alternative.id: One recipe with the looped run

open-question.alternative: The two become one execution recipe as in the merged option, holding the Claude Code `high`, Antigravity `high`, and Claude Code `xhigh` lines with the duplicate Antigravity critical copy dropped. `Execute tasks one at a time` (its slot line `<single-task line>`) joins that recipe as one more variant instead of standing as a recipe of its own. The named single-task lines stay separate recipes, as the rule file and the preview reference them by heading. The execute-tasks step shows a single button covering every way the shipped file runs a mission's tasks, whole-list or looped. Choosing how tasks are run becomes one consistent dropdown choice. One button's variants would then behave differently on click: three start a run at once, while the looped variant opens the preview (`previewLoop`) instead of posting `runRecipe`. The page and pane would have to branch per variant where today they branch per recipe. The slot line also carries no harness, model, or effort for the label to show or for the settings view to edit, which depends on how the unreadable-lines question is settled. On top of this, it carries the merged option's remembered-difficulty and lost-name costs.

open-question.question: Variants edited in the settings view are to be stored as literal lines in a per-user file. The one per-user file today is a person's hand-written own recipe file (`~/.gurita/recipes.md`, moved by the setting `gurita.ownRecipesFile`), which the extension reads and never writes. Which file holds the variants the settings view writes, that own recipe file or a new file of the extension's own, and in what format?
open-question.alternative: The own recipe file stays read-only, and the settings view writes a new file of the extension's own in the same recipe Markdown format, such as `~/.gurita/variants.md` beside the own file (in the directory `gurita.ownRecipesFile` names, or at a fixed path). The extension is that file's only writer and renders it whole on each save. The recipe reader reads it as a third source beside the shipped and own files, in one fixed order of precedence. A person's hand-written file is never written, so nothing they typed can be lost. The store still reads as plain recipes that a person can inspect, copy into their own file, or edit by hand, and the existing reader parses it with no second format. It adds a third recipe source and a precedence rule between it, the own file, and the shipped file. A person can now define one recipe in two per-user files, and must know which file wins and which one the settings view changed. Its contents and precedence depend on the sibling questions of whether a stored copy stands in for a shipped variant (Shipped variant editing) and whether an own recipe replaces a shipped one or joins it (Own recipe replacement).

The settings view writes into the person's own recipe file (`~/.gurita/recipes.md`, or wherever `gurita.ownRecipesFile` points), which stops being read-only to the extension. The format is the recipe Markdown the reader already parses: `###` headings, an optional `Stage:` line, and fenced blocks of literal lines, with variants written the way the shipped file writes them. Each edit is a byte-preserving splice. Only the recipe or variant it changes is touched, a new one is appended, and every other byte of the person's text, including their prose, comments, and layout, is written back unchanged. The file is created, with `~/.gurita/`, the first time a variant is stored. One per-user file and one reader serve both hand-written and settings-view variants, so what the settings view stores is exactly what a person would have written by hand and can keep editing in a text editor. No new path, setting, or second source is added to the shipped-then-own order the reader already follows. The extension now writes a file the person authors by hand. It needs a splice writer that finds one variant's block inside free-form Markdown without disturbing anything else, and it has to handle a hand edit made while the pane is open. What it writes into that file depends on how the sibling questions settle the variant syntax (Shipped variant format) and whether an own recipe of a shipped name replaces the shipped one or joins it (Own recipe replacement).

The settings view writes into the person's own recipe file, in the same recipe Markdown format, but only inside one section that belongs to the extension, a fixed `##` heading the extension creates at the end of the file. It rewrites that section whole on each save and never touches anything outside it. A person's hand-written recipes stay where they stand and are never edited by the settings view. A variant the settings view stores under a name that also has a hand-written recipe sits in the managed section, and the reader resolves the two by a fixed order between the hand part and the managed part. One file and one reader still hold everything, while the extension's writes stay inside a region it owns. It needs no splice into free-form text, and a person's own prose and recipes are never rewritten. Hand-written and settings-view entries for the same recipe can stand side by side in one file. The reader needs a precedence rule between the two parts of one file, and a person who edits the managed section by hand has those edits overwritten on the next save. The precedence rule interacts with the sibling question of whether an own recipe replaces a shipped one or joins it (Own recipe replacement).

The settings view writes into the person's own recipe file in the recipe Markdown format and re-renders the whole file in one canonical layout on every save, untouched recipes included. It parses the file and writes it back the way the task-list tool renders `TASKS_TODO.md`, so drift in blank lines, fences, or ordering is normalized silently, and any prose outside recipe blocks is dropped or moved. It has the simplest writer of the own-file options: parse, change, render. It never has to locate a byte range in hand-written text, and the file always reads in one predictable shape. The first save through the settings view rewrites text the person wrote by hand. Notes, comments, ordering, and layout that the reader ignores are lost or normalized, and unlike the plugin's task list no commit records what was dropped, since the file stands outside any repository. The rendered syntax depends on the sibling question of how variants are written (Shipped variant format).

The own recipe file stays read-only, and the settings view writes a new JSON file of the extension's own at a visible per-user path beside the own file, such as `~/.gurita/variants.json`. It holds structured records, each a recipe name, a variant name, its literal lines as an array of strings, and which variant is the default. The extension is its only writer, reads it with `JSON.parse`, and merges it with the recipes the Markdown reader yields. A structured file matches what the settings view edits: names, an ordered list of lines, and a default flag. Reading and writing need no Markdown parsing or splicing, and the file still sits at a visible path a person can back up, inspect, or carry to another machine. Variants then live in two formats, Markdown recipes in the shipped and own files and JSON records here. A variant cannot move between the store and a hand-written recipe file without converting it, and the JSON is awkward to edit by hand, with escaped quotes in every command line. Its precedence against the other sources depends on the sibling questions Shipped variant editing and Own recipe replacement.

The own recipe file stays read-only, and the settings view writes a new JSON file of structured records (recipe name, variant name, literal lines, default) inside the extension's global storage directory (`ExtensionContext.globalStorageUri`), a per-user location that VS Code owns and that is not in the home directory. VS Code provides and owns the location, so the extension creates no directory in the person's home and its private store cannot collide with anything a person keeps under `~/.gurita/`. The store is hidden, so a person cannot easily find, back up, or hand-edit their variants. It is kept per editor profile, it is removed when the extension is uninstalled, and other editors and the command line cannot read it. Like the home-directory JSON file, it adds a second format beside the Markdown recipes, and its precedence depends on the sibling questions Shipped variant editing and Own recipe replacement.

No recipe file is written. The variants are stored in VS Code's user `settings.json` as a new setting the manifest contributes at application scope beside `gurita.ownRecipesFile` (such as `gurita.variants`), holding an array of records with a recipe name, a variant name, the literal lines as strings, and the default. The extension writes them through the configuration API, and the own recipe file stays read-only. VS Code's own writer does the writing, so the extension adds no file, path, or atomic writer. The setting appears in the Settings editor and travels between machines through Settings Sync, like the one setting the extension already has. A file the person shares with every other extension and hand-edits as JSONC then holds blocks of quoted command lines. Large structured values are awkward in the Settings editor, and the store depends on how the configuration API rewrites that file. Like the JSON files, it adds a second format beside the Markdown recipes. Whether it fits depends on where the sibling question puts the settings view's harness values (Harness state store).

open-question.question: The extension is to read each line's harness, model, and effort from the line's own text. A variant may hold a line that carries none of them or not all: a shell step of the person's own, the looped recipe's slot line `<single-task line>`, a command of a harness the extension does not know, or a harness line written without `--model` or `--effort`. How is such a line treated on the recipe button and in the settings view's line editor?
open-question.alternative: On the recipe button, each line adds only the values its text carries: a `claude` or `agy` line without `--model` or `--effort` adds its harness and whichever flag it holds, while a shell step, the slot line `<single-task line>`, and a line of a command the extension does not know add nothing, so a variant none of whose lines is readable, the shipped looped recipe among them, shows its name alone. In the line editor, only a line of a known harness carrying both `--model` and `--effort` gets model and effort controls; every other line is shown as its text, read-only. The extension never invents a value and never writes a flag a line did not already carry, so the only rewrite it makes is replacing a value already in the text, the smallest step away from the draft's rule that it composes no line. The button silently understates what a variant runs: it cannot tell a harness's default model from a line that runs no harness at all, and the looped recipe's button says nothing of what its tasks run on. A harness line written without a flag can never be given a model or effort in the settings view.

On the recipe button, each line adds the values it carries and a fixed mark for each gap: `default` for a model or effort a known-harness line leaves out, one fixed mark (such as "other step") for a shell step or a line of a command the extension does not know, and one fixed mark (such as "per task") for the slot line `<single-task line>`. In the line editor, only a line of a known harness carrying both `--model` and `--effort` gets model and effort controls; every other line is shown as its text, read-only. The button tells the person truthfully what each part of a variant runs on, including that a step runs outside any harness or on the harness's own default, while the extension still writes only values already in a line. The marks are a small vocabulary of their own to name, draw, and test, and they lengthen labels whose shape the button-label sibling decides. A flagless harness line stays uneditable, so the person must hand-write the flag in an own recipe to get controls.

On the recipe button, each line adds the values it carries and a fixed mark for each gap: `default` for a model or effort a known-harness line leaves out, one fixed mark for a shell step or a line of a command the extension does not know, and one fixed mark (such as "per task") for the slot line. In the line editor, every line of a known harness gets model and effort controls, a missing value shown as the harness default, and setting one inserts the flag into the line's text ahead of its closing `;` and any `# interactive` comment; every other line is shown as its text, read-only. Every line that runs a harness the extension knows can have its model and effort set, so no hand-written line is a dead end in the editor, and the button says what each gap means. The extension composes text into a line rather than only replacing a value, so it must know where a flag goes in a hand-written line and can malform one whose shape it misjudges, and it moves furthest from the draft's rule that the extension composes no line.

On the recipe button, each line adds only the values its text carries, a shell step, the slot line, and a line of an unknown command adding nothing. In the line editor, every line of a known harness gets model and effort controls, a missing value shown as the harness default, and setting one inserts the flag into the line's text ahead of its closing `;` and any `# interactive` comment; every other line is shown as its text, read-only. The button stays as short as the values written allow and needs no mark vocabulary, while the editor lets the person write the missing flag, after which the button shows it. The button cannot tell a harness default from a step outside any harness, and the looped recipe's button shows its name alone; the editor still composes text into hand-written lines, with the misplacement risk that carries.

On the recipe button, each line adds the values it carries and a fixed mark for each other gap (`default` for a missing model or effort on a known harness, one fixed mark for a shell step or a line of an unknown command), while the slot line `<single-task line>` adds the harness, model, and effort read from the named single-task lines the looped run may choose for a task. In the line editor, only a line of a known harness carrying both flags gets model and effort controls; every other line, the slot line included, is shown as its text, read-only. The looped recipe's button shows the models and efforts its tasks can actually run on, the one recipe whose single line otherwise says nothing about them. Drawing the button needs the single-task lines, and for an exact set the rule file's assignments, read at every redraw, and the values shown are per task rather than per variant, so the label can name combinations a given run never uses; how single-task lines appear in the settings view is a sibling's choice this leans on.

alternative.id: Resolve slot line, editor adds flags

open-question.alternative: On the recipe button, each line adds the values it carries and a fixed mark for each other gap (`default` for a missing model or effort on a known harness, one fixed mark for a shell step or a line of an unknown command), while the slot line adds the harness, model, and effort read from the named single-task lines the looped run may choose. In the line editor, every line of a known harness gets model and effort controls, a missing value shown as the harness default, and setting one inserts the flag ahead of the line's closing `;` and any `# interactive` comment; every other line, the slot line included, is shown as its text, read-only. The fullest reading: every button says what each line runs on, the looped recipe included, and every known-harness line can have its model and effort set. It carries both costs at once: the button depends on reading the single-task lines and rule file at every redraw, and the editor composes flags into hand-written lines it may misplace, the largest departure from the draft's rule that the extension composes no line.

open-question.question: On Antigravity the efforts a model takes differ by model: `gemini-4-argon` and `claude-opus-5-5` stop at `high`, while `gemini-4-neon` and `gemini-4-hydrogen` go up to `xhigh`, and a line naming an effort its model lacks stops when run. Is a harness's effort list one list for the whole harness, offered for every line, or kept per model, so that a line is offered only the efforts its model takes?
open-question.alternative: Each harness holds one effort list for the whole harness, and the line editor offers that whole list for every line of the harness whatever its model. The settings view holds no record of which model takes which effort, and a line given an effort its model lacks is accepted by the editor and stops when it is run, as a hand-written line does today. The simplest store and editor: one flat list per harness, matching the shape `claude --help` gives (one effort set, no per-model listing) and the lists the goal already names, with no per-model structure to keep, migrate, or fill in for models nobody uses. On Antigravity the editor offers `xhigh` and `max` for `gemini-4-argon` and `claude-opus-5-5`, which stop at `high`, so the settings view lets a person save a variant that is known to fail, and the failure shows only at run time, possibly part-way through an unattended chain.

Each harness keeps a list of models, each model carrying its own effort list, on both harnesses, and the line editor offers a line only the efforts its model takes. When a line's model is changed to one whose list lacks the line's current effort, or a stored or shipped line already names such an effort, the effort is kept as written and drawn marked as not taken by its model until the person picks one of the offered values. A line edited in the settings view cannot be given an effort its model lacks, matching the per-model pairs `agy models` prints (an effort-less id such as `gemini-pro-orchestrator-neon` carrying an empty list), while nothing the person wrote is changed without their action and a mismatch already present is visible rather than hidden. Every model needs its own effort list, which on Claude Code no command reports, so the per-model lists there are either copies of one set or entries someone must keep; how they are filled turns on the sibling list-source question, and the editor and store need a model-to-efforts structure and a marked state for a mismatched line.

alternative.id: Per model, effort reset on model change

open-question.alternative: Each harness keeps a list of models, each model carrying its own effort list, on both harnesses, and the line editor offers a line only the efforts its model takes. When a line's model is changed to one whose list lacks the line's current effort, the effort is replaced at once by the highest effort the new model takes that does not exceed the old one (the model's lowest when none is lower), so every line the editor saves names an effort its model takes; a stored or shipped line already naming such an effort is drawn marked until edited. A model change can never leave a line in a state that fails at run time: switching `gemini-4-neon` at `xhigh` to `gemini-4-argon` yields `high` in one step, with no second pick needed. The editor changes a value the person did not touch, so a quiet downgrade (an `xhigh` task line becoming `high`) can go unnoticed and run at less effort than intended; it carries the same per-model lists, and the same dependence on the sibling list-source question for Claude Code, as any per-model option.

Each harness holds one effort list for the whole harness, and any model of that harness may optionally carry its own narrower effort list; the line editor offers a line its model's own list when the model has one and the harness list otherwise. A line whose current effort its model's list lacks keeps it as written, drawn marked as not taken, until the person picks an offered value. Restrictions are recorded only where a model is known to differ (the Antigravity models that stop at `high`), so Claude Code and any model without known limits stay one flat list, while the known Antigravity failures are still kept out of the editor. Two levels of list and a fallback rule between them make the store and the editor more involved than either pure form, and a model with no subset of its own is offered the whole harness list even when it in fact takes less, so the protection is only as complete as the subsets someone has entered or read, which turns on the sibling list-source question.

The granularity is fixed per harness rather than chosen once: Antigravity keeps an effort list per model, in the pairs `agy models` prints, and the line editor offers an Antigravity line only its model's efforts, while Claude Code holds one effort list for the whole harness offered for every Claude Code line. An Antigravity line whose current effort its model lacks keeps it as written, drawn marked, until the person picks an offered value. Each harness's list takes the shape that harness itself reports, per model where `agy models` gives the pairs and one set where `claude --help` gives one, so the settings view never asks anyone to invent per-model effort lists Claude Code gives no source for. The two harnesses are stored and edited in different shapes, so the editor carries two code paths and a third harness (whether Codex is covered is a sibling question) must be assigned one; a Claude Code model that does not take every listed effort is still offered all of them.

open-question.question: The settings view checks each harness by finding its CLI through a shell and reading its installed plugins from the harness's own `plugin list` command, so every check starts an interactive shell and a harness process. When does the check run: each time the settings view is opened, with every re-read of the pane, or only when the person asks for it?

recommendation.option: Once per pane, lazily, with re-check

open-question.recommendation: Only a person who opens the settings view pays for the shell and the harness processes, and once per panel, so moving in and out of the view to edit variants never waits on an unchanged result. The check-again control serves the one moment a fresh result matters, after installing or upgrading from a terminal, and nothing outside the view needs the result earlier.

alternative.id: Once per pane, lazily, with re-check

open-question.alternative: The check runs the first time the settings view is opened after the panel is created, and its result is cached for the panel's lifetime, shown on every later opening without running again; a check-again control in the settings view re-runs it on request, and no pane re-read or Refresh runs it. The cost is paid once per panel and only by a person who actually opens the settings view, while every later opening is instant and the person can still re-check after installing or upgrading a plugin. A result taken earlier in the session can be stale without sign (a plugin upgraded from a terminal reads old until the person presses the control or reopens the panel), and nothing is known about any harness until the settings view has been opened once, which fails if the failed-check consequence or the initial enabled state (both siblings' questions) needs the result on the mission pages.

The check of every harness runs afresh each time the person opens the settings view, its results drawn as they arrive and held only while the view stays shown; nothing is cached between openings, no separate check control is added, and reopening the view is the way to check again. No other re-read of the pane runs it. What the view shows is always as current as the moment it was opened, so a harness or plugin installed or upgraded from a terminal shows correctly the next time the view is opened, with no control to learn and no cached state to go stale. Every opening pays one interactive shell, whose startup files run each time, and one `plugin list` process per harness (66 entries for `claude` here, and a Codex listing that ran over a minute without `-m gurita`), so a person moving in and out of the view to edit variants waits on the same unchanged result again and again; and the result exists only while the view is open, which fails if the failed-check consequence (a sibling's question) has it act on the mission pages too.

The check runs as part of every full re-read of the pane (its opening, the Refresh control and command, a hidden stale panel shown again, a run's terminal closing, and a watcher burst that moves the live list), its results posted with each redraw; the watcher's in-process re-reads of one mission's documents do not run it, and the settings view shows the result of the latest full re-read. The results are always present wherever the pane draws, and they refresh after every run's terminal closes, so a Gurita copy installed or upgraded by a recipe run is picked up with no action of the person's, ready for any use the mission pages make of it. The heaviest cadence: a shell and harness processes start on every run's end and every Refresh, mostly to read a result that has not changed, and the check's latency or failure is tied to the re-read that draws the missions, so a slow harness listing can hold back or complicate every redraw of the pane.

alternative.id: Once per pane, eagerly, with re-check

open-question.alternative: The check runs once in the background when the panel is created, independently of the settings view and of the first mission read, its result cached for the panel's lifetime; the Refresh control and command and a check-again control in the settings view re-run it, while the watcher's re-reads, a hidden panel shown again, and a run's terminal closing do not. The result is ready before the person opens the settings view and available to the mission pages from the start, at one check per panel plus explicit re-checks, without paying a shell on every run's end. Every panel opening pays the shell and harness processes whether or not the settings view is ever used, and a plugin upgraded by a recipe run or a terminal reads stale until the person refreshes or re-checks.

Nothing runs the check automatically: the settings view shows each harness as not yet checked until the person presses a check control there, which checks every harness and shows the result until the panel closes or the control is pressed again. No shell or harness process ever starts unless the person asks, so opening the pane or the settings view costs nothing extra and a slow or broken harness listing can never delay anything the person did not request. The view opens with no answer to its main question, every new panel needs a press before the harness state is known, and a person who never presses it never learns of a missing or outdated copy, which leaves nothing to act on if the failed-check consequence or the initial enabled state (siblings' questions) relies on a check result.

The latest check result is stored so that it outlasts the panel and the editor session, shown in the settings view with the time it was taken; the check runs automatically only when no stored result exists, and otherwise only when the person presses a check-again control. Across sessions the check costs almost nothing, since a harness setup changes rarely, while the settings view and the mission pages always have a result to show from the first moment. The stored result goes stale silently whenever a CLI, plugin, or the extension itself is upgraded, so the check reports what was true at some past time, and it adds stored state the extension holds nowhere today, its location depending on where the settings view's other values are kept (the harness state store, a sibling's question).

open-question.question: The settings view enables or disables each harness, and a variant's lines each run on one harness, a variant sometimes mixing two. What does disabling a harness do to the variants holding a line that runs on it: are they left out of the recipe dropdowns, listed but not runnable, or still runnable under a mark?
open-question.recommendation: Disabling then means one plain thing, that the list offers nothing running on that harness, and it clears away the copies a person does not use, the job the host groups did. The pane's existing check against the posted list enforces it with no new non-runnable state, and since a harness is hidden only by the person's own act, a variant never vanishes for a reason they did not cause.
open-question.alternative: A variant that has at least one line on a disabled harness is left out of its recipe's dropdown, mixed variants included. The pane leaves it out of the list it posts, so a click on it is refused the way a click on any name the posted list lacks is refused now. A recipe whose every variant is left out loses its button. Where the default or remembered variant is left out, the button runs the default if that variant is still listed and otherwise the first listed variant. The remembered selection is kept and comes back once the harness is enabled again. The page offers only what can run on the harnesses the person has chosen. A person who has no Antigravity, or does not want it, gets one list with nothing in the way, and the pane's existing check against the posted list stops a hidden variant from running with no new runtime guard. A variant vanishes with nothing on the page to say why, so a person who forgot they disabled a harness sees a recipe lose a variant, or disappear, and has to work out the cause from the settings view. A mixed chain such as the Gemini-reviews, Claude-annotates review is lost whole because of one harness, even though most of its lines would run.

A variant is left out of its recipe's dropdown only when every one of its lines runs on a disabled harness. A variant mixing a disabled harness with an enabled one stays listed and runnable as it is, with no mark, and its disabled-harness lines run when the chain reaches them. Hidden variants, recipes with nothing left, and the fallback for a hidden default or remembered variant work as in the any-line option: the posted list leaves them out, a recipe with no variant left loses its button, the default is used if still listed and otherwise the first listed variant, and the remembered selection is kept for re-enabling. Disabling a harness clears the single-harness copies away, which is most of what the Antigravity copies are, while keeping the one deliberately mixed chain, whose whole point is to use both harnesses, available. Disabling does not fully hold: a listed variant can still start a harness the person disabled, with no sign of it on the button, so "disabled" means "mostly hidden" and not "never run". The rule also depends on every line's harness being read, so its edge depends on how the Unreadable lines question treats a line that names no harness.

A variant that has at least one line on a disabled harness stays in its recipe's dropdown, drawn as a non-runnable entry that names the disabled harness, as a recipe holding an unknown placeholder is drawn now. When it is the selected variant, the button is drawn disabled with that reason beside it. The pane also refuses a run of it, so a stale page cannot start one. A recipe whose every variant is affected keeps its button, drawn disabled. The default and the remembered selection stay as they are, so re-enabling the harness makes the same variant runnable again with nothing re-chosen. Disabling is enforced, and it is also visible where its effect is felt: the person sees what exists, why it will not run, and which setting to change. This follows the page's existing practice for a recipe it cannot run. The page keeps showing entries the person said they do not use. A person who never runs Antigravity has every dropdown padded with dead variants and may see recipe buttons that are permanently disabled. It also adds a second non-runnable state to draw, explain, and test alongside the unknown-placeholder one.

A variant that has at least one line on a disabled harness stays in its recipe's dropdown and stays runnable. Its dropdown entry, and the button while it is selected, carry a mark naming the disabled harness. A click starts the run at once, as every recipe click does now, with no confirmation and no refusal. The default and the remembered selection are unaffected. Nothing the person might need is ever taken away or blocked. The mark warns them, and they stay free to run a variant anyway, for instance a harness they disabled only to declutter the settings view's checks. Disabling becomes a label and not a control, so a person who disabled a harness because it is not installed or not trusted can still start it with one click. Every affected variant also stays in the way. It sits close to whatever mark a failed check gets, which the Failed check consequence question owns, so the two marks need to be told apart.

Disabling a harness changes nothing on the mission pages: every variant is listed, runnable, and unmarked whatever its harness. The enabled state acts only inside the settings view, where it stops that harness's check from running and collapses or greys out its model and effort lists, while that harness's lines stay editable. It is the smallest change. The recipe list's drawing, the pane's posted list, and its run guard need no harness test at all, and enabling a harness never has to be reconciled with a remembered or default selection. The setting no longer does what a person would expect from "disable". The page goes on offering every Antigravity copy beside its Claude Code one, which is the clutter the goal's harness settings were plausibly meant to remove. The settings view also gains a switch whose whole effect is cosmetic inside that view.

open-question.question: Today a recipe in a person's hand-written own recipe file that carries a shipped recipe's name replaces that recipe whole and in place. Once a recipe carries variants, what does a hand-written own recipe of a shipped recipe's name do: replace every variant of that recipe, or join them as one more variant?
open-question.alternative: An own recipe carrying a shipped recipe's name replaces that recipe whole and in place, every shipped variant included, as `mergeRecipes` does today. The own recipe is read by the same rule as the shipped file, so it brings its own variants when it writes several and is a recipe of one variant when it writes one block. No shipped variant of that name stays on the button, a fixed-name button recipe included. It keeps today's rule and the README's description unchanged in meaning: the name stays the recipe's only identity, the merge stays one lookup by name, and a person who wants a shipped variant beside their own copies it into the same own recipe, so what the button offers is exactly what that file says. A person who wants only to add one variant must copy every shipped variant into their own file to keep it, and those copies stop following the shipped file when a later version changes them; how heavy that is depends on the sibling question of which file the settings view writes its variants to.

An own recipe carrying a shipped recipe's name never replaces anything: its block, or each of its variants when it writes several, joins the shipped recipe as one more variant, listed after the shipped variants under its own variant name and marked as the person's own, a same-named variant kept as a second entry rather than taking the shipped one's place. The shipped variants all stay on the button. Adding a variant costs one block in the own file, with nothing copied, so every shipped variant keeps following the shipped file across versions while the person's own sits beside them in the same dropdown. A person can no longer take a shipped variant away or change one in place by hand, since a same-named own variant only stands beside it, so a recipe whose shipped variants a person never wants keeps offering them; it also changes what an existing own recipe of a shipped name does, from replacing the recipe to adding to it, without any edit to the file.

An own recipe carrying a shipped recipe's name is merged into it variant by variant: an own variant carrying a shipped variant's name replaces that variant in place, and every other own variant joins after the shipped ones. The shipped variants the own recipe does not name stay as they are, and the own recipe always writes its variants in the shipped file's variant form, each named. It gives both moves with no extra syntax, overriding one shipped variant or adding one, while every variant the person did not touch keeps following the shipped file, which matches the variant-grained edits the settings view makes. The name now has to be matched at two levels, recipe and variant, so a mistyped variant name silently adds a variant instead of replacing one, a person cannot remove a shipped variant without some further rule, and the own file has to spell variant names in whatever form the sibling question on the shipped variant format settles.

An own recipe carrying a shipped recipe's name declares what it does, through one line between its heading and its block like the existing `Stage:` line: one value makes it replace every variant of the shipped recipe, the other makes its variants join the shipped ones, and a recipe declaring nothing takes one fixed default of the two. Each person chooses per recipe between taking a recipe over and adding to it, so neither the copying cost of whole replacement nor the inability to remove shipped variants under joining is forced on everyone. It adds a second declaration line the reader must parse, the README must document, and a person must know about, and which of the two behaviours the undeclared default takes still has to be chosen, an existing own recipe falling under it unchanged.

An own recipe no longer touches a shipped recipe of its name: the shipped recipe keeps all its variants, and the own recipe of the colliding name is drawn as a non-runnable entry naming the collision and its file, as a recipe with an unknown placeholder is drawn today, so a hand-written recipe must take a name of its own. Changing a shipped recipe's variants is left to the settings view alone. A name then means exactly one recipe, so the pane's start-by-name check, the fixed-name buttons, and the merge need no rule for a collision, and the settings view becomes the one place a shipped recipe's variants are changed. It removes a capability the extension ships today, replacing a recipe by hand, the seven fixed-name button recipes included, and turns every existing own recipe of a shipped name into a dead entry; it is viable only as far as the settings view's own edits reach shipped variants, which the sibling question on editing shipped variants settles.

open-question.question: Variants are to be stored as literal lines in a per-user file. Where are the settings view's other values kept, each harness's enabled or disabled state and its model and effort lists: in that same per-user file, in VS Code user settings, or in the extension's own stored state?
open-question.alternative: All harness values are contributed configuration properties of the extension (for example one object per harness under a `gurita.` key), at application scope like the existing `gurita.ownRecipesFile`, and the settings view writes them to the user's global settings through the configuration API; the per-user file holds only variants. VS Code's own mechanism: a schema in the manifest validates the values, the person can read and edit them in `settings.json` or the Settings editor, the extension is told of changes made there, and Settings Sync carries the lists to every machine the person uses. The settings view's values are split across two stores, a file and settings, with no single place to see them together; object-valued settings show in the Settings editor only as an "Edit in settings.json" link; and syncing carries a harness's enabled state to machines where that harness is not installed, so its variants may show as enabled where they cannot run.

Each harness's enabled or disabled state and its model and effort lists are kept in the same per-user file that holds the variants, in a part of that file set aside for harness values, so the settings view reads and writes one file for everything it holds; nothing goes into VS Code settings or the extension's stored state. One store for the whole settings view: one file to read on every re-read of the pane, one write path, one place a person can open, back up, copy to another machine, or fix by hand, and a variant's model and effort sit beside the lists they are chosen from. The file must carry structured values that are not recipe lines, so its format has to hold a second kind of content and its reader must survive hand edits to it; how awkward that is depends on which file holds the variants and in what format (the Variant store file question), being worst if that is a person's hand-written Markdown recipe file. A machine-specific fact like whether a harness is enabled also travels wherever the file is copied.

All harness values are contributed configuration properties written to the user's global settings, but each harness's enabled state is declared at machine scope, so it stays on the machine where it was set, while the model and effort lists are at application scope and sync; the per-user file holds only variants. Keeps every value in VS Code's validated, hand-editable settings while matching each to what it describes: whether a harness is enabled follows what is installed on this machine, and the lists, a person's preferences, follow the person. Two scopes to declare, explain, and test, on top of the split between settings and the variant file; a person setting up a second machine re-enables harnesses there; and the scope rules are VS Code behaviour the extension's tests, which run against a stub of the `vscode` module and never inside an editor, cannot exercise.

All harness values are kept in the extension's own global state (`globalState`, the store VS Code keeps per extension), written and read only by the extension, not synced across machines unless keys are registered for sync; the manifest contributes no new setting and the per-user file holds only variants. Nothing a person can break by hand and no schema or file format to define: the settings view is the one writer and reader, values are typed objects the code stores directly, and the stub-based tests can stand in for the store with a plain map. The values are invisible outside the settings view: a person cannot read, diff, back up, or copy them, they are lost with the extension's storage (an uninstall, a new profile), and the variants in a file can then name models the lost lists no longer hold. The extension today uses no stored state at all, so this adds a third kind of storage beside the recipe files and the one setting.

All harness values are kept in a second per-user file of the extension's own, separate from the variant file (for example beside it under `~/.gurita/`), in a format chosen for structured values, which the settings view writes and a person may edit by hand; nothing goes into VS Code settings or stored state. A plain, hand-editable, copyable file outside VS Code, as the variants are, without forcing structured harness values into the variant file's format, so each file keeps one kind of content and its own simple reader. A second file the extension writes and must read robustly against hand edits, with a second path to default and perhaps a second setting to move it, for what may be only a handful of values; whether that cost is worth paying depends on how many values there are to keep, which turns on whether the lists are person-editable (the Model and effort list source question). Its enabled state, like the variant file's contents, travels wherever the file is copied.

alternative.id: Enabled in state, lists in file

open-question.alternative: Each harness's enabled or disabled state is kept in the extension's global state, per machine and unsynced, while the model and effort lists are kept with the variants in the per-user file; the manifest contributes no new setting. Each value lives where its nature points: the enabled state, a fact about this machine's installed harnesses, stays on the machine and needs no format, while the lists, which the variants' lines are edited against, stay beside those variants in the one file a person can read and copy. Two stores for one view, one of them invisible, so a person reading the file sees the lists but not which harnesses are enabled; the variant file still has to carry a second kind of content, with the same dependence on that file's choice and format (the Variant store file question).

open-question.question: The settings view enables or disables each harness, and the looped task run is to stay as it is. Does disabling a harness reach beyond the mission page's recipe list, to the seven fixed-name buttons, whose shipped lines all run on Claude Code, and to the named single-task lines the looped run's preview offers and its rules choose?
open-question.recommendation: Disabling takes over what the host groups did, choosing which harness copies the recipe list offers, and hiding has no sensible form for a fixed-name button or a rule-chosen line, where it would remove a control or stop a run. The buttons keep running the variant their recipe's default names, and the looped run stays as the goal keeps it.
open-question.alternative: Disabling a harness acts on the mission page's recipe list alone. The seven fixed-name buttons run their recipes as today whatever harness their lines name, and the looped run's single-task lines are untouched: the preview's override list offers every named single-task line, the rules choose among all of them, and every line is still passed to the runner as one `--line`. The two surfaces the goal keeps as they are, the looped run and the fixed-name buttons, which `pane.ts` resolves through `BUTTON_RECIPES` outside the list, need no change at all. The setting means one plain thing: which harnesses the recipe list offers. A disabled harness still runs from seven buttons and from every looped task its rules or a person's override send to it. Disabling Claude Code, the harness every shipped button line and two of the three shipped single-task lines run on, would leave most of what the pane can start running on it, so the setting reads as broader than it is.

Disabling a harness acts on the recipe list and on the seven fixed-name buttons, each button treated by the harness its recipe's lines run on, the same way the list treats a variant. The looped run's single-task lines are untouched: the override list offers every one, the rules choose among all of them, and every line still reaches the runner. Every recipe a person starts by a click on the page follows the setting, while the looped run, its rule file, and the runner stay exactly as the goal keeps them, so no question arises about what a rule naming a disabled line should do. With every shipped button line on Claude Code, disabling it changes all seven buttons at once unless an own recipe of the same name runs them elsewhere. How a button is treated depends on the sibling axes of whether button recipes carry variants and on what disabling does to a variant. A looped run still sends tasks to a disabled harness.

Disabling a harness acts on the recipe list and on the menu the looped run's preview offers: the override list's choice of named single-task lines treats a line on a disabled harness as the list treats a variant. The rules' own choices are untouched, every single-task line is still passed to the runner, and a task the rules send to a disabled line still runs on it. The fixed-name buttons are untouched. What a person can choose follows the setting at both places where they choose a run's harness, while the rule file's assignments, `loop.ts`'s `--line` set, and the runner behave exactly as today. It is a half-reach: a run whose rules pick a disabled line still runs on that harness although the person could not choose it in the preview's menu, so the setting holds for overrides and not for the defaults beside them. The seven buttons still ignore it.

Disabling a harness acts on the recipe list, on the preview's override list, and on the single-task lines the rules choose: the preview treats a task whose rule-chosen line runs on a disabled harness the way the list treats a variant, so the run cannot start, or shows that task marked, until the person overrides it to an enabled line, without a change to the rule file or the runner. The fixed-name buttons are untouched. No looped task can reach a disabled harness without the person seeing it, so the setting holds for every run of more than one task, the place where a wrong harness costs the most. It changes how the looped run starts, which the goal keeps as it is, and leaving a line out of the `--line` set `loop.ts` passes would make a rule naming it fail in the runner, so the reach has to stop at the preview. The seven buttons still run on a disabled harness.
